newsitem.title: GERMANY: German churches rail against unemployment.
newsitem.headline: German churches rail against unemployment.

text.p: German Roman Catholic and Protestant churches leaped into a heated debate over the country's stalled economic reform with a joint warning on Friday on the evils of mass unemployment and excesses of capitalism.

Leaders of the German Catholic Bishops' Conference and Protestant Churches in Germany said the 12.2 percent unemployment rate was a catastrophe and urged the government to work with industry and labour to find a new consensus to solve economic problems.

"Work is a human right and we cannot allow ourselves to simply accept the fact that this right is being denied to more than one-tenth of our workforce," Klaus Engelhardt, chairman of the Council of Protestant Churches, told a news conference.

The churches, which enjoy a strong social standing in Germany, presented 258 suggestions in a 103-page paper they said would help the government, industry and society overcome the economic troubles plaguing the country.

They issued the warning as Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right coalition leaders met opposition Social Democrats (SPD) in Bonn to discuss a package of economic reforms aimed at lowering unemployment from the current 4.66 million.

"The churches can no longer turn their backs to the challenges such as unemployment, just distribution of wealth, the social state...and globalisation of markets," said Bishop Karl Lehmann, chairman of the German Bishops' Conference.
"Some have apparently forgotten the most important thing, that the human being is the common standard for everything -- not the free market," he added.

In their paper, the two churches argued that Germany's so-called "social market economy" should not be blamed for the current economic malaise, but instead the high unemployment was robbing the country of its economic vitality.

The "social market economy", which combines a free market economy with generous safety nets and considerable government guidance, has served Germany well and was a key ingredient for West Germany's post-war "economic miracle".
But economists and industrialists say pressures from global competition have eroded Germany's economic position.

In their joint statement, the churches criticised the globalisation for having a "destablising effect on national economies" and called for measures that would put a better framework on "the high and permanently rising sums that are changing hands in international financial markets."

Saying Germany needed "less state and more people taking responsibility for themselves", the churches were strongly opposed to "pure capitalism". They also decried a rise in poverty in Germany in recent years and bemoaned the lingering rifts between east and west Germany.

"The state, the economy and the society have to be rearranged in a way to overcome these problems," said Bishop Josef Homeyer of Hildesheim. "Pure capitalism is a horrible mistake and can't be reconciled with Christian traditions."

The major political parties in Bonn welcomed the churches' message, with the Christian Democrats (CDU), the SPD, Free Democrats (FDP) and Greens all finding elements that matched their proposals on the tax and economic reform.
"The churches now have to actively work with us on cutting unemployment," said Guido Westerwelle, FDP general secretary.

Rudolf Scharping, SPD parliamentary leader, pointed to the church's admonition on the state to ensure fair distribution between haves and have-nots. And Kohl's CDU also felt their position backed by the church.
"It is an urgently needed appeal for solidarity and justice rather than a society run by selfishness and people with sharp elbows," said Herman-Josef Arentz, a CDU parliamentarian.
